title: Why couldn’t these users find the command?
answer: All six gave up at least once, each time on a menu command

checks.question: A later build adds a visible Undo button beside the folder path, outside the Main Menu. Which observation in this study suggests that would help, and what could a six-person study of the old build not tell you?
checks.answer: The people who gave up on Undo did not open the Main Menu, so a button they can see removes the step they skipped. The study cannot say how many users would still miss it: six first-time users of one test build give no rate, and the new design needs its own test.

checks.question: P5 gave up on Select All but had no difficulty with Undo; P1 had no difficulty with Select All but gave up on Undo. What does that suggest about explaining the give-ups by who was skilled?
checks.answer: Skill alone would make the same people fail on both. Instead each person stalled on a different command, and all six stalled at least once, which points at where particular commands sat and at habits such as Ctrl+A, not at a few weak users.

checks.question: P6’s attempt at Select All is gray, outside the study’s scope. If it were counted as a give-up instead, how would the ranking of tasks by give-ups change, and why does the report keep gray separate?
checks.answer: Select All would have four give-ups and be worst on its own, ahead of Undo’s three. The report keeps gray separate because the study excluded that approach, so scoring it either way would rank tasks on something the study did not test.

steps.title: P1 gave up on Undo
steps.line: The command was there: Undo was in the Main Menu.
steps.caption: The task read: Undo an action with the “Undo/Redo” button. This schematic shows where the command sat; it is not a screenshot of Files. None of those who gave up opened the Main Menu, where Undo was. The command existed, and P1 still did not find it. Was P1 unlucky, or did the same menu lose other people too?
steps.picture: Main menu. Undo. Task: Undo the move. P1 could not complete it.

steps.title: Three of the six gave up on Undo
steps.line: The others: one no difficulty, two very little difficulty.
steps.caption: The same task split the six people, graded with the report’s colours; an approach outside the study’s scope counts as neither a success nor a give-up. If a few weaker users caused the trouble, the same names would keep failing. The next step tests that across all eleven tasks.
steps.picture: P1. Could not. complete. P2. Very little. difficulty. P3. Could not. complete. P4. Very little. difficulty. P5. No. difficulty. P6. Could not. complete.

steps.title: All six gave up at least once, each time on a menu command
steps.line: Black cells are give-ups: 11, in 5 tasks and all six columns.
steps.caption: No small group accounts for the give-ups: every one of the six gave up at least once, P4 and P5 once each. All 11 came on menu tasks, though nine of the eleven tasks used menus. The report’s reasons point at where the commands sat: those who quit Undo never opened the Main Menu, those who quit Select All reached for Ctrl+A or dragging, and those who quit Open Item Location had not checked the file’s right-click menu.
steps.picture: Give-ups by task and participant, P1 outlined: 1 Change the icon size: P2 and P6 gave up; 3 Select All: P3, P4 and P5 gave up; 4 Undo the move: P1, P3 and P6 gave up; 7 Open Item Location: P1 and P2 gave up; 9 Add To Bookmarks: P3 gave up. Give-ups per participant: P1 2, P2 2, P3 3, P4 1, P5 1, P6 2; 11 in all. No one gave up on the other 6 tasks.
